Radar absorbing materials (RAMs) have been researched actively for over four decades.
RCS reduction techniques include shaping, active loading, discrete loading, and distributed loading with RAMs.
The first patented RAM was a quarterwave resonant material developed in the Netherlands in 1936 operating near 2 GHz.
Germany developed Wesch material and Jaumann absorbers during World War II for submarine stealth.
The US developed HARP paints and Salisbury screens as early RAMs in the 1940s and 1950s.
Salisbury screens use a resistive sheet spaced a quarter wavelength from a metal surface to achieve resonance.
Broadband RAMs were achieved by multilayering resonant absorbers and using bulk absorbers with carbon-infused matrices.
Circuit analog RAMs (CA-RAM) use patterned lossy films to tailor impedance and reduce thickness.
Magnetic RAMs such as ferrites operate at lower frequencies but are heavier and degrade at higher frequencies.
Biochemical compounds discovered in the 1980s exhibit ultrawideband absorption and are lighter than ferrites by a factor of 10.
Chiral RAMs utilize optical activity and circular dichroism to achieve polarization-independent ultrawideband absorption.
The transmission line approach models RAM as a lossy matching network to calculate reflection coefficients.
For zero reflection, the RAM input impedance must match the free space impedance (377 ohms) and be frequency independent.
Analysis of RAM on curved surfaces involves theorems by Weston and requires considering specular and diffracted fields.
Computational methods like MOM, FDTD, GO, and GTD are used for RAM analysis depending on frequency and geometry.
Ideal RAMs for aerospace have low density, high mechanical strength, and chemical resistance to fuels and fluids.
Reflection coefficients of -20 dB or lower indicate effective absorption in RAM materials.
Multilayer RAMs can broaden absorption bandwidth by stacking layers with different electromagnetic properties.
The refractive index and characteristic impedance of RAM materials are complex and frequency dependent.
Loss tangents quantify the dielectric and magnetic losses critical for RAM performance.
